Learning Objectives
Explain the interplay between hip osteology and soft-tissue anatomy and hip dislocations and
associated injuries.
Recognize the clinical and imaging study findings of simple hip dislocations.
Appreciate treatment algorithms for the management of acute hip dislocations and their
sequalae.
Review the prognosis and pathophysiology of complications after hip dislocation.


Overview
Traumatic dislocation of the hip is an orthopaedic emergency typically caused by high-
energy trauma. Substantial force is required to dislocate the femoral head from the
acetabulum, and associated injuries are common. Traumatic hip dislocation can be
divided into simple and complex dislocations. Simple dislocations do not have an
associated fracture, whereas complex dislocations occur in combination with femoral
head, femoral neck, and/or acetabular fractures. Most hip dislocations occur posteriorly;
however, the femoral head also may be displaced inferiorly (obturator dislocation) or
anteriorly. Urgent reduction is the priority of management to preserve blood supply to
the femoral head, followed by management of concomitant soft-tissue and osseous
pathology. Patient outcomes largely depend on the development of osteonecrosis of the
femoral head, arthritis, heterotopic ossification, and sciatic nerve palsy.
Epidemiology/Etiology
Traumatic dislocations of the hip are severe injuries that primarily occur in young patients as a
result of high-energy trauma.
These injuries most commonly result from motor vehicle collisions. Falls from a height and
sporting injuries are other common mechanisms of injury.
Dislocations can be isolated or can occur with associated fractures of the femoral head,
femoral neck, or acetabulum.

Epidemiology/Etiology
Traumatic hip dislocations are potentially devastating injuries that primarily occur in
younger patients after high-energy trauma. Most hip dislocations occur in males aged 16
to 40 years, with motor vehicle collisions accounting for more than two-thirds of these
injuries.1 A substantial amount of force is required to dislocate the hip; therefore, it is a
sign of severe orthopaedic and non-orthopaedic injuries. The most common type is a
posterior dislocation, which occurs in approximately 90% of patients. Approximately 70%
of dislocations are associated with acetabular fractures.2 The mechanism of injury often

9/3/26, 4:22 PM

https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6002099
2/32

involves an axial load through the femur, and the direction of dislocation is dictated by
the position of the limb at the time of injury.
Anatomy and Biomechanics
Osteology
The hip is a ball-and-socket joint, and the bony architecture provides inherent stability.
Stability is augmented by the ligamentous capsule, labrum, and muscular attachments.
The mean femoral neck-shaft angle is 130° with 15° of anteversion; however, considerable
variability exists.
Femoroacetabular impingement, increased neck-shaft angle, and acetabular retroversion
increase the risk of dislocation without associated fracture (Figure 1).
Figure 1 Illustrations of a hip show pincer impingement (A), cam impingement (B), and
combined impingement (C). (Reproduced from Mulcahey MK, Byrd JWT: Femoroacetabular
impingement. OrthoInfo. Rosemont, IL, American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons, August
2020. Available at: https://orthoinfo.aaos.org/en/diseases--conditions/femoroacetabular-
impingement/. Accessed January 18, 2023.)

Osteology
The hip is a multiaxial ball-and-socket joint designed for weight bearing, motion, and
stability. Dissimilar from the shoulder, the hip has considerably more surface area
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:22 PM
AAOS | Hip Dislocations
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6002099
3/32

between the ball and socket. Soft tissues, such as the fibrocartilaginous labrum,
transverse acetabular ligament, and hip capsule, provide additional stability. The
acetabulum almost entirely encompasses the hemispheric femoral head. The lunate
surface of the acetabulum is covered by hyaline cartilage and is broadest superiorly.
With the exception of the fovea, the insertion site of the ligamentum teres, the femoral
head also is covered by hyaline cartilage. Because of the intrinsic stability of the hip,
traumatic dislocation invariably results in damage to the articular and periarticular
structures of the hip. Morphologic osseous characteristics, including cam deformity,
increased neck-shaft angle, reduced femoral anteversion or femoral retroversion,
acetabular retroversion, and dysplasia, increase the risk of traumatic posterior
dislocation without fracture.3-5 With increasing hip flexion and internal rotation,
interaction between the femoral neck and the prominent acetabular rim may act as a
fulcrum, making these hips more susceptible to traumatic dislocation.3 Hips with this
fulcrum may dislocate with lower force injury and will more likely dislocate without a
fracture if the posterior rim is less prominent (Resource 1).
Vascular Anatomy
The major blood supply to the femoral head is the medial femoral circumflex artery (Figure 2).
Lesser vascular contributions come from the lateral femoral circumflex artery and the artery of
the ligamentum teres, a branch of the obturator artery.
Disruption of the blood supply to the femoral head during hip dislocation likely is a substantial
factor in the development of osteonecrosis.

the femoral head, which arises from the medial and lateral circumflex vessels. These vessels
create a ring, giving rise to the cervical vessels. A minor contribution comes from the obturator


Vascular Anatomy
An understanding of the blood supply to the femoral head is crucial in the management
of traumatic hip dislocations. In adults, the medial femoral circumflex artery provides the
main blood supply to the proximal femur, supplying approximately 82% of the femoral
head and 67% of the femoral neck. The deep branch of the medial femoral circumflex
artery runs along the inferior border of the obturator externus before perforating the
hip capsule just cranial to the insertion of the tendon of the superior gemellus. It then
splits into two to five retinacular vessels that run cranially over the posterosuperior
aspect of the femoral neck.6 These vessels enter the femoral head at the bone-cartilage
junction. Dislocation may cause direct trauma or temporary tamponade of the vessels,
compromising the vascular supply to the femoral head. Additional contributions come
from the obturator and lateral femoral circumflex arteries. The artery of the ligamentum
teres, a branch of the obturator artery, provides substantial perfusion to the femoral
head in children but comprises only approximately 10% of the femoral head blood
supply in adults. The ligamentum teres and this arterial branch are almost always injured
in patients with a traumatic hip dislocation; however, the clinical consequences of such
injury is unknown.
Relevant Soft-Tissue Anatomy
The hip capsule is reinforced by strong capsular ligaments, including the iliofemoral,
ischiofemoral, and pubofemoral ligaments that extend from the acetabulum to the femoral
neck (Figure 3).
The ligamentum teres runs from the cotyloid fossa of the acetabulum to the fovea centralis of
the femoral head.
The rim of the acetabulum is raised by a fibrocartilaginous collar, the acetabular labrum, which
deepens the acetabulum and provides additional stability.

Figure 3 Anterior (A) and posterior (B) view illustrations show the hip capsule and its
thickenings (ligaments). (Reproduced from Scolaro JA: Hip dislocations and femoral head
fractures, in Lieberman JR, ed: AAOS Comprehensive Orthopaedic Review, ed 3. Rosemont, IL,
American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons, 2020, pp 1001-1007.)

Relevant Soft-Tissue Anatomy
The capsule of the hip joint is thick, fibrous tissue that attaches medially to the labrum
and the margin of the acetabulum. Laterally, it extends to the intertrochanteric line
anteriorly and to the neck of the femur just proximal to the intertrochanteric line
posteriorly. Three stout ligaments reinforce the fibrous capsule: the iliofemoral,
ischiofemoral, and pubofemoral ligaments. The iliofemoral ligament (Y-ligament of
Bigelow) originates on the anterior acetabulum and fans out to a broad insertion on the
anterior femoral neck. The ischiofemoral ligament reinforces the posterior aspect of the
capsule, attaching from the ischium to the posterior aspect of the femoral neck. The
pubofemoral ligament comprises the anteroinferior capsular thickening. The
fibrocartilaginous labrum deepens the acetabulum, enhances stability, and maintains
the vacuum seal of the joint. Inferiorly, the labrum bridges across the acetabular notch
as the transverse acetabular ligament. The ligamentum teres is a flat band of delicate
tissue that connects the cotyloid fossa of the acetabulum to the fovea of the femoral
head. It carries a small branch of the obturator artery. Injury to this arterial branch is
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:22 PM

https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6002099
7/32

clinically unimportant; however, the ruptured ligament may be the cause of mechanical
hip pain in some patients.
Etiology/Mechanism of Injury
The direction of force and the position of the limb at the time of injury determine the direction
of dislocation and associated fractures.
Posterior hip dislocations result from an axial load through the femur with the hip in a flexed,
adducted, and internally rotated position. This mechanism of injury is commonly observed if
the knee strikes the dashboard in a high-energy motor vehicle collision.
Anterior hip dislocations occur if the hip is abducted, extended, and externally rotated at the
time of injury.

Etiology/Mechanism of Injury
Hip dislocations result from high-energy sports injuries, falls from a height, and work-
related accidents because than 400 N of force are required to dislocate the hip joint.7
Posterior dislocations, caused by adduction, internal rotation, and flexion of the hip at
the time of trauma, represent most injury patterns. Posterior dislocations are most
commonly observed after dashboard injuries, in which the knee strikes the dashboard,
resulting in a posteriorly directed force through the femur. An alternative hypothesis is
that the mechanism of injury involves a posteriorly directed force vector from the vehicle
driver depressing the brake pedal with the hip in a flexed and adducted position.8
Anterior hip dislocations can be subdivided into superior and inferior types.
Anterosuperior dislocations are caused by abduction, external rotation, and extension of
the hip. Anteroinferior dislocations are caused by abduction, external rotation, and
flexion of the hip. Central dislocations involve a fracture of the quadrilateral surface and
frequently result from a direct blow or a fall directly onto the greater trochanter. The
presence, location, and extent of an associated fracture is dictated by the position of the
leg at the time of the impact and a patient’s bony morphology of the proximal femur and
acetabulum.

Associated Injuries
Approximately 70% to 95% of patients with a traumatic dislocation have additional associated
injuries, orthopaedic and non-orthopaedic in nature.
Acetabular fractures are observed in approximately 70% of patients with a hip dislocation.
Femoral head fractures occur at high rates in patients with a hip dislocation, and the location
of the fracture is based on the direction of dislocation.
A high incidence of ligamentous injury to the ipsilateral knee has been reported. Many of these
injuries are missed on initial assessment.
The peroneal division of the sciatic nerve is the most commonly associated neurologic injury
that is observed in patients with a hip dislocation, occurring in approximately 10% of patients.

Associated Injuries
Hip dislocation frequently is associated with additional injuries. The most common
concomitant injury observed in patients with a hip dislocation is an acetabular fracture,
occurring in approximately 70% of patients.1,9,10 Femoral head and femoral neck
fractures may be a component of the injury pattern and may be difficult to recognize on
initial plain radiographs. Femoral head fractures occur in 7% to 16% of patients with a
posterior hip dislocation.1,11 Typically, the anteromedial femoral head fractures from
shear forces as the femoral head displaces past the posterior wall of the acetabulum.12
Anterior dislocation of the hip is associated with a higher likelihood of femoral head
fracture, and the fracture usually is an infra-foveal impaction fracture13 (Resource 2).
The axial load on the femur that results in a hip dislocation often is transmitted through
the knee, with 25% of patients with a hip dislocation presenting with ipsilateral knee
injuries.14 Although a thorough physical examination of the knee often is difficult in
patents with a hip dislocation, a high suspicion for ipsilateral knee injuries is required on
initial trauma evaluation (Resource 3).
Peripheral nerve injury is rare, with an incidence of approximately 10%. The peroneal
distribution of the sciatic nerve is the most common nerve involved. This results from
direct pressure of the head of the femur on the nerve or stretching of the nerve based
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:22 PM
AAOS | Hip Dislocations
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6002099
9/32

on abnormal tension on the soft tissue in patients with a dislocation.15 Direct vascular
compromise is uncommon but may result from arterial or venous occlusion.
Associated upper and lower extremity fractures are observed in 20% and 36% of
patients, respectively.10 Other common non-orthopaedic injuries include closed head
injury and abdominopelvic trauma. The reported death rate in patients who sustain a
traumatic hip dislocation during a motor vehicle collision ranges from 2.3% to 6%.10,16
The use of airbags and seat belts greatly reduces the risk of serious injury.10 Several
studies suggest that traumatic hip dislocation is associated with a poorer prognosis in
patients who sustain multiple traumatic injuries.17
Injury Classification
Hip dislocations are classified as anterior, posterior, or obturator dislocations based on the
direction of displacement of the femoral head (Figures 4, 5 and 6).


Injury Classification
Various classification systems exist, encompassing simple and complex hip dislocations.
The Thompson-Epstein classification of posterior hip dislocations is the most widely used
classification system. Type I dislocations are those with or without a minor fracture. Type
II dislocations occur in combination with a single large fracture of the posterior rim of
the acetabulum. Type III dislocations occur in combination with a comminuted fracture
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:22 PM
AAOS | Hip Dislocations
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6002099
15/32

of the rim with or without a large major fragment. Type IV dislocations occur in
combination with a fracture of the acetabular floor. Type V dislocations occur in
combination with a fracture of the femoral head. The Pipkin classification system is used
for the classification of femoral head fractures that often occur in patients with a
traumatic hip dislocation (Resource 4).
Evaluation/Diagnosis
Physical Examination
Advanced Trauma Life Support protocol should be part of the initial assessment of any patient
with a hip dislocation.
Native hip dislocation is an orthopaedic surgical emergency. Timely diagnosis and reduction
are critical.
Patients with a posterior hip dislocation present with a leg that is flexed, adducted, internally
rotated, and short.
Patients with an anterior hip dislocation present with the leg in abduction and external
rotation.
Patients with an irreducible dislocation present with the hip in slight but fixed flexion and
immobile neutral rotation, which differs from passive hip mobility observed in patients with a
classic anterior or posterior dislocation.
A thorough neurovascular examination and radiographic workup should be performed before
any reduction is attempted.

Physical Examination
Patients with a traumatic hip dislocation require a complete assessment based on
Advanced Trauma Life Support protocol, with a thorough physical examination to assess
for concomitant injuries. Physical examination should be performed to evaluate the soft
tissue. The position of the leg often will reveal the direction of dislocation. The classic
appearance of a posterior hip dislocation is a leg that is flexed, adducted, internally
rotated, and shortened. In patients with an irreducible or locked hip dislocation (with or
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:22 PM
AAOS | Hip Dislocations
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6002099
16/32

without a fracture), the hip and knee are commonly slightly flexed with the leg shortened
and in neutral rotation.11 Conversely, patients with an anterior hip dislocation present
with the leg in abduction and external rotation. A high percentage of patients sustain
associated ipsilateral knee pathology; therefore, physical examination of the knee should
be performed on initial trauma assessment and after hip reduction. Delayed diagnosis of
clinically important ipsilateral knee injuries is common and substantially affects
rehabilitation.14 A thorough neurovascular examination should be performed before any
reduction attempt. Failure to recognize a hip dislocation promptly and consequent
delayed reduction are associated with a substantially poorer prognosis.
Imaging Studies
Radiography
Every trauma evaluation should begin with an AP pelvis radiograph.
If concern for hip dislocation exists based on initial AP radiographs or the clinical examination,
orthogonal radiographs of the affected hip, femur, and knee should be obtained.
Multiple radiographic views should always be obtained so subtle abnormalities are not missed.
Femoral head and neck fractures may not be easily visualized on radiographs, and advanced
imaging studies are required after reduction.

Imaging Studies
Typically, hip dislocation is initially diagnosed via standard AP radiographs. Findings may
be subtle; therefore, radiographs must be scrutinized. If concern for hip dislocation
exists based on initial AP radiographs or clinical examination, then orthogonal
radiographs of the affected hip, femur, and knee should be obtained. In posterior
dislocations, the femoral head appears smaller than the contralateral hip (if unaffected)
on a standard AP radiograph and typically is located superiorly. The femur usually is in
adduction and internal rotation; therefore, the lesser trochanter will be less visible than
usual. Occasionally, the femoral head is dislocated directly posteriorly and may appear
to be reduced in the acetabulum. In anterior dislocations, the femoral head appears
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:22 PM
AAOS | Hip Dislocations
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6002099
17/32

larger and overlaps the medial acetabulum or the obturator foramen. A cross-table
lateral radiograph should be used to confirm the direction of dislocation.
Judet radiographs (iliac and obturator oblique views) provide additional information on
the location of the dislocation and can be obtained to identify associated acetabular
pathology. Associated femoral head or femoral neck fractures may be visualized on
radiographs; however, advanced imaging studies should always be obtained after
reduction to ensure nondisplaced fractures are not missed or to further characterize
fractures observed on post-reduction radiographs. The unusual injury pattern of an
irreducible femoral head fracture-dislocation is identified via close apposition of the
cancellous surface of the dislocated proximal femoral head against the lateral iliac
cortical bone of the supra-acetabular region.
Computed Tomography
Reduction of simple dislocations and fracture-dislocations should not be delayed to obtain a
CT scan.
CT scan of the pelvis are obtained after successful hip reduction and before surgical
management.
A CT scan provides important information about concentricity of reduction, bony fragments
within the joint, and articular impaction of the femoral head or the acetabulum, as well as
acetabular, femoral head, or neck fractures.
In patients with an irreducible dislocation, valuable information can be obtained via a
preoperative CT scan regarding a block to reduction or associated fracture of the femoral head
and/or neck.

Computed Tomography
A fine-cut CT scan of the pelvis (2- to 3-mm maximum slice thickness) should be obtained
after closed reduction to verify a concentric joint, diagnose associated fractures, or
identify loose fragments in the joint that may not have been appreciated on initial
radiographs. A CT scan of the pelvis should be obtained rather than a CT scan of the
involved hip so that the contralateral side may be used for comparison. A widened hip
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:22 PM
AAOS | Hip Dislocations
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6002099
18/32

joint space may indicate soft-tissue interposition from a capsule or labral tear. A CT scan
is necessary to characterize femoral head, femoral neck, or acetabular fractures for
surgical planning. This advanced imaging study details the location of fracture
fragments, detects femoral head or acetabular impaction, and identifies joint debris.
These variables associated with hip dislocation ultimately determine the course of
management. 
Magnetic Resonance Imaging
The role of MRI after simple hip dislocation is controversial.
In the acute setting, MRI may help to identify damage to the labrum, articular cartilage, or
loose chondral fragments.
Additional research is necessary to determine if MRI performed at the time of simple hip
dislocation is cost-effective and changes management.
MRI is useful in the subacute period after injury to diagnose early-stage osteonecrosis of the
femoral head, before the onset of radiographic changes are visible. This may help facilitate
joint-preserving techniques.

Magnetic Resonance Imaging
MRI provides the greatest visualization of soft-tissue injury after hip dislocation;
however, which patients require MRI and at what point MRI is required postinjury has
yet to be established.18,19 MRI may be helpful in evaluating a widened hip joint if CT
does not identify the etiology. In addition, MRI provides superior definition of chondral
loose bodies and capsular and labral injuries compared with CT. Intra-articular
fragments may accelerate chondral damage and increase the risk of osteoarthritis;
therefore, their identification and timely removal are paramount. MRI in the acute
setting of a hip dislocation does not replace the established algorithm of conventional
radiography and CT.6 Occasionally, hemodynamic instability and other injuries and
patient specifics do not allow for MRI in the acute setting. The authors of this lesson
prefer to perform MRI acutely if it will affect management.6
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:22 PM
AAOS | Hip Dislocations
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6002099
19/32

MRI is the preferred imaging modality for the diagnosis of osteonecrosis of the femoral
head, particularly in early stages in which radiographs may appear normal.18
Osteonecrosis manifests as pain and stiffness weeks to months postinjury. MRI can
provide early information on the quality of the femoral head articular cartilage and may
allow for joint preservation techniques.
MRI also can be performed to evaluate the ipsilateral knee, if deemed necessary based
on a patient’s clinical history or physical examination. Schmidt et al14 prospectively
evaluated the ipsilateral knee of patients who sustained a traumatic hip dislocation and
found that 21% of patients had a cruciate ligament injury. Physical examination of the
ipsilateral knee in patients with a hip dislocation often is difficult because of limited hip
motion, generalized pain, and muscle spasm resulting in guarding. Examination under
anesthesia may help elucidate knee instability but may result in other injuries, such as a
meniscal tear, partial ligament disruption, or extensor mechanism injury, being missed.
MRI is sensitive and specific in the identification of intra-articular abnormalities that may
not be identified via patient history and physical examination alone. Early diagnosis of
injuries allows for appropriate management or rehabilitation protocols to be more
rapidly initiated, which may lead to improved functional outcomes.
Management
Closed Reduction
Closed reduction should be attempted within 6 to 12 hours postinjury to decrease the risk of
osteonecrosis.
Adequate sedation is essential to overcome the strong musculature.
Closed reduction is performed via inline traction and re-creation of the mechanism of injury.
After closed reduction, radiographs and CT scans should be obtained to confirm concentric
reduction and characterize associated fractures.
Closed reduction may be unsuccessful because of inadequate sedation, entrapment of the
femoral head in a capsular injury, femoral head impaction onto the acetabular rim, or
additional bony and ligamentous injuries preventing effective manipulation of the extremity.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:22 PM
AAOS | Hip Dislocations
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6002099
20/32

If closed reduction cannot be achieved with the use of sedation in the trauma bay, the patient
should be taken to the operating room for closed reduction under anesthesia, with the
surgeon prepared to attempt more invasive techniques.

Closed Reduction
On identification of a hip dislocation, closed reduction should be promptly performed
because timing affects the outcome of these injuries.20-22 The timing of hip reduction is
an important variable in the management of hip dislocations because displacement of
the femoral head compromises blood supply. Reduction is performed via inline traction
on the lower extremity and re-creation of the position of the limb at the time of injury,
with a slow constant force that fatigues the musculature of a relaxed patient. The goal is
to complete a reduction without incurring additional articular or bony injuries. Adequate
sedation and pharmacologic muscle relaxation are essential.
Several reduction maneuvers have been described. The most commonly used technique
for posterior dislocations is the Allis maneuver. The patient is placed in the supine
position with the pelvis stabilized; the hip is flexed, adducted, and internally and
externally rotated with constant inline traction, allowing the femoral head to clear the
posterior wall of the acetabulum. For anterior dislocations, traction should be applied,
followed by external rotation and hip extension. Stability of the reduction should be
assessed while the patient is sedated. The hip should be tested in neutral, abduction,
and adduction in full extension and in 90° of flexion. Skeletal traction is indicated for
patients who have an unstable reduction, injuries with acetabular dome involvement, or
free fragments in the joint.8 Concomitant fractures of the acetabulum and femoral head
are not contraindications to attempting closed reduction. After successful closed
reduction, radiographs and CT scans should be obtained to confirm reduction and
identify associated femoral head or acetabular fractures. Radiographs should be
scrutinized for subtle signs of a widening hip joint, which may indicate capsular or labral
tissue interposition.
If reduction under conscious sedation is unsuccessful, additional manipulation should
not be performed to avoid additional trauma to the hip.1 Excessive force should be
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:22 PM
AAOS | Hip Dislocations
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6002099
21/32

avoided because this may lead to iatrogenic femoral head and/or neck fractures.
Reasons for unsuccessful reduction include inadequate sedation; entrapment of the
femoral head through the capsule, labrum, tendon, or fascia; or ipsilateral injuries that
prevent effective traction and manipulation of the limb. The patient should be taken to
the operating room for attempted closed reduction under general anesthesia with
paralysis. The surgeon should be prepared to perform open reduction. Approximately
2% to 15% of hip dislocations are irreducible via closed means.21,22
Nonsurgical Management
Indications
Simple hip dislocations without persistent instability can be managed nonsurgically.
Dislocations with a small avulsion fracture of the caudal posterior wall can be managed
nonsurgically.
Nonsurgical management is acceptable in a concentrically reduced hip with a femoral head
fracture that is infra-foveal, displaced less than 1 mm, and not associated with intra-articular
debris.
No consensus exists with regard to restrictions or physical therapy after reduction of traumatic
hip dislocation; however, patients usually are progressed to weight bearing as tolerated with
hip precautions based on the direction of dislocation.

Indications
If post-reduction radiographs and CT scans show concentric reduction without fracture,
the patient is eligible for nonsurgical treatment. Examination under anesthesia may
afford useful information if concern for persistent instability exists after closed
reduction, particularly in patients with a small posterior wall fracture. Patients with a
cranially located posterior wall fracture near the weight-bearing dome are more likely to
have persistent instability than patients with a caudal fracture.23 If physiologic force can
produce any subluxation of the femoral head, then repair of the injured structures is
necessary. Patients with normal hip morphology and a small, caudal posterior wall

and/or a small, nondisplaced infra foveal femoral head fracture can be treated using the
same algorithm as that for simple dislocations.9 Closed treatment is appropriate in
patients with a concentrically reduced hip with a femoral head fracture that is non–
weight bearing, displaced less than 1 mm, and not associated with intra-articular debris.
The clinical importance of loose bodies below the fovea is unknown.24
Weight-bearing and activity restrictions after closed reduction of a simple hip dislocation
are controversial. For many years, prolonged immobilization or traction were
recommended; however, recent studies have reported improved outcomes with early
mobilization.2 The main goal is prevention of osteonecrosis of the femoral head and
osteoarthritis; however, research on specific rehabilitation methods and restrictions is
lacking. Most protocols advocate for early active range of motion with hip precautions to
prevent at-risk leg positions. For posterior dislocations, hip hyperflexion, adduction, and
internal rotation are avoided. A brief period of toe-touch weight bearing (4 weeks) is
advanced to weight bearing as tolerated.8 Prospective studies are necessary to
determine the development of osteonecrosis and posttraumatic arthritis and the correct
post-reduction precautions and protocols after a simple hip dislocation.
Surgical Management
If reduction is unattainable via closed means, then percutaneous or open techniques must be
used.
Knowledge of the potential block to reduction is imperative.
Open reduction usually is approached from the direction of the dislocation.
Management of complex hip dislocations generally is predicated on the specific management
of the associated fracture (femoral neck, femoral head, acetabulum).
Hip arthroscopy can be used to repair the labrum or remove small entrapped osseous and
cartilage fragments from within the hip joint, especially if open surgical management is not
otherwise indicated.

Absolute indications for acute surgical management after hip dislocation include
irreducible dislocations and nonconcentric reductions. A preoperative CT scan should be
obtained promptly to delineate the specific block to reduction and characterize
associated fractures. Percutaneous reduction often is attempted first. A Schanz pin may
be placed in the proximal femur to allow for better manipulation, particularly in patients
with a diaphyseal femur fracture. If open reduction of a simple dislocation is required,
the hip usually is approached from the direction of the dislocation. Typically, posterior
dislocations are approached via a Kocher-Langenbeck or a modified Gibson exposure,
whereas anterior dislocations are approached via a Hueter exposure. Interposed soft
tissues are removed, the joint is inspected for loose bodies, the hip is reduced, and the
soft tissues are inspected and repaired. The posterior wall and the posterior column of
the acetabulum are best accessed via the Kocher-Langenbeck approach. The Hueter
approach also allows for visualization of femoral neck and anteroinferior femoral head
fractures. A modified Gibson surgical hip dislocation with a digastric osteotomy is a
powerful approach that can be used to manage head fractures and many acetabular
fractures. It is the most useful approach to manage cranially located posterior wall
fractures. In removing articular debris, surgeons must scrutinize preoperative CT scans
to understand the number and locations of the fragments to ensure removal of all
fragments.
Hip arthroscopy after a simple hip dislocation is beneficial for the removal of loose
bodies and to manage articular pathology, including labral tears, chondral damage, and
ligamentum teres tears that have failed nonsurgical management.25 A high index of
suspicion for loose bodies should be maintained in patients with persistent mechanical
symptoms after hip dislocation.24 A systematic review of 151 patients who underwent
hip arthroscopy after hip dislocation found a high rate of intra-articular fragments
(89.3%), many of which were not visualized on preoperative CT scans.19 Arthroscopic
management is limited by the amount of articular damage sustained during dislocation
or reduction. Defects in the femoral head and the acetabular cartilage are observed in
almost all patients who undergo arthroscopy after hip dislocation and occasionally can
be managed arthroscopically. Osteochondral defects and labral pathology can be
managed via open surgical techniques, depending on the patient and specific injury.

Rapid posttraumatic arthritis often develops in patients with the most severe intra-
articular chondral damage.26
Outcomes
Few studies have documented the long-term outcomes after a simple hip dislocation.
The outcomes after a simple hip dislocation vary widely. Outcomes are influenced by time to
reduction, the extent of concomitant injuries, and the condition of the hip before dislocation.
Outcomes largely depend on the development of osteonecrosis, arthritis, heterotopic
ossification, and sciatic nerve palsy.

Outcomes
Historically, simple dislocations without fracture were thought to be easily managed via
closed reduction and result in minimal long-term complications. Currently, practitioners
recognize that even with prompt reduction, complications, such as osteonecrosis,
posttraumatic arthritis, sciatic nerve palsy, and mechanical symptoms, can occur.
Prognosis after traumatic dislocation is extremely varied and depends on time to
reduction, cartilage injury, associated fracture, and the presence of polytrauma.9 In
general, anterior dislocations are associated with a better prognosis than posterior
dislocations. Dreinhofer et al9 reported on 50 patients with a hip dislocation, all of which
were reduced within 6 hours postinjury. At a mean follow-up of 8 years, good or
excellent results were observed in 14 of the 30 posterior dislocations compared with 9 of
the 12 anterior dislocations. Long-term results of 74 patients with a simple traumatic hip
dislocation revealed that 24% of the patients had substantial residual pain and
disability.27 Even the patients with a hip classified as satisfactory at final follow-up had
pain, discomfort, and limitations after prolonged walking or exercise. Sahin et al2
reported on 62 patients with a dislocation or fracture-dislocation at a mean follow-up of
9.6 years. Very good or good-to-medium results were reported in 71% of the patients,
and the time between injury and reduction correlated with long-term prognosis.

Acetabular fracture-dislocations are associated with a poorer prognosis compared with
simple hip dislocations.
Complications
Osteonecrosis
Many studies have attempted to examine the pathoetiology and causative nature of
posttraumatic osteonecrosis. These studies appear to support an acute vascular stretch and
twisting injury with delayed thrombosis and fibrosis.
Osteonecrosis generally is thought to occur within 2 years of dislocation; however, it has been
reported to occur as long as 8 years after dislocation.
Rates of osteonecrosis vary widely in the literature. If the hip is reduced within 6 hours
postinjury, the rate of osteonecrosis is approximately 2% to 10%. The risk of osteonecrosis is
increased if the hip remains dislocated for a prolonged period but also may be affected by the
direct impact of the initial injury.

Osteonecrosis
Osteonecrosis of the femoral head is a severe complication that results in collapse of the
femoral head, fragmentation of the articular cartilage, and secondary hip arthritis. The
exact pathophysiology of osteonecrosis is unknown; however, the dislocation event has
been hypothesized to cause stretching and tamponade of the retinacular vessels to the
femoral head. Strong data link osteonecrosis of the femoral head to the time interval
from injury to hip reduction and the severity of injury.
Rates of osteonecrosis after traumatic hip dislocation vary among studies and range
from 1% to 50%;2,9,21,22,27 however, this rate can be substantially decreased if reduction
is performed within 6 hours postinjury. Evidence shows that time to reduction in
patients with a traumatic hip dislocation is critical, and the longer a hip remains
dislocated, the higher the risk of osteonecrosis. Early reduction may resume blood flow
to the femoral head by relieving tension across the retinacular vessels. Prolonged
dislocation results in irreversible ischemia. In a meta-analysis of five studies, including

reduction groups were 36.4% and 8.2%, respectively. Patients who sustained a high-

with patients who sustained a low-energy mechanism of injury (47% versus 7.5%,
respectively), even if reduction was performed less than 12 hours postinjury. Although
prompt reduction alone does not ensure excellent outcomes, delayed reduction of
traumatic hip dislocations is clearly associated with an increased risk for osteonecrosis.
Arthritis
Posttraumatic arthritis occurs in approximately 20% of patients who sustain a simple hip
dislocation, a rate five times higher than that in the general population.
The increased rate of posttraumatic arthritis after traumatic dislocation likely results from
articular cartilage injury during the initial dislocation; however, unrecognized loose bodies may
play a role.

Arthritis
Posttraumatic arthritis is the most common long-term sequelae of simple hip
dislocation. Because of the intrinsic stability of the hip, traumatic hip dislocation
invariably results in damage to articular cartilage. Similar to osteonecrosis, the incidence
of posttraumatic arthritis is higher in patients who sustain multiple traumatic injuries
than in those with an isolated injury.9 Posttraumatic arthritis is more common in
patients with a posterior dislocation than in those with an anterior dislocation and is
more common in patients with a fracture-dislocation than in those with a simple
dislocation. Posttraumatic arthritis can rapidly develop in patients with severe intra-
articular chondral damage. Unmanaged intra-articular bodies accelerate chondral
damage and increase the risk of osteoarthritis.

Heterotopic ossification results from a combination of muscle contusion from the initial injury
and surgical trauma.
Heterotopic ossification more often occurs after extensile approaches to the femoral head and
the acetabulum.
The use of prophylactic indomethacin or radiation therapy may reduce the rate of clinically
significant heterotopic ossification formation.
Substantial heterotopic ossification formation may lead to stiffness and, in rare cases, late
sciatic nerve dysfunction.

Heterotopic Ossification
Heterotopic ossification is the pathologic formation of bone in extra skeletal tissue.
Heterotopic ossification is a known complication of surgical approaches to the hip that
involve dissection of the gluteal muscles but also may occur after traumatic injury to the
muscles from hip dislocation. The mechanism of heterotopic ossification involves
differentiation of mesenchymal stem cells into osteoprogenitor cells within the muscle;
however, the exact pathway has yet to be elucidated. Risk factors for heterotopic
ossification include traumatic brain injury, spinal cord injury, male sex, and acetabular
fracture.28 Indomethacin and single-dose radiation therapy provide effective prophylaxis
against heterotopic ossification formation. Heterotopic ossification often is
asymptomatic; however, if formed in bulk in the abductor muscles, it may present as
substantial hip stiffness. In rare cases, heterotopic ossification can cause compression of
the sciatic nerve, leading to late sciatic nerve dysfunction.15
Neural Injury/Nerve Palsy
Nerve palsy after traumatic hip dislocation results from direct pressure of the femoral head on
the nerve or associated soft-tissue stretching.
The sciatic nerve, usually the peroneal division, is the most commonly injured.
Sciatic nerve palsy is more common with fracture-dislocations than simple dislocations.
At least partial recovery of nerve function occurs in 60% to 70% of patients who undergo
nonsurgical treatment.

Neural Injury/Nerve Palsy
Neurologic function should be assessed on initial evaluation of patients with a traumatic
hip dislocation. As soon as possible after reduction, neurologic function of the limb
should be reassessed. A 10% incidence of nerve injury has been reported after traumatic
hip dislocation, most commonly involving the peroneal distribution of the sciatic nerve.
The sciatic nerve can be stretched; compressed; or, rarely, acutely lacerated. Major nerve
injury is much more common in patients who are transferred before hip reduction (16%)
compared with patients with a hip dislocation that is reduced before transfer (4%),
highlighting that the time to reduction substantially affects outcomes.8 If a sciatic nerve
palsy is persistent after reduction or present in an irreducible hip, the lower extremity
should be placed in a position of hip extension and knee flexion, if possible, to reduce
tension on the sciatic nerve.
Functional recovery is related to the degree of initial nerve injury, with complete palsies
resulting in a poorer prognosis than partial palsies. At least partial recovery of nerve
function occurs in 60% to 70% of patients, with no clear correlation between injury and
type of management.8,15 An ankle-foot orthosis can aid in ambulation. If recovery does
not occur, patients may be offered tendon transfer at the ankle. In patients with late
sciatic nerve compression resulting from heterotopic ossification or scar formation,
neurolysis is effective in regaining at least some nerve function; however, nerve
exploration is associated with a risk of iatrogenic nerve injury.
